summary: This memo discusses subnets, parts of one Internet network that are logically visible as separate pieces, and proposes procedures for using them, including how to handle routing. Organizations used subnets instead of getting many separate network numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: One big neighborhood gets split into smaller streets, each handled separately, so you do not need a whole new town for every street.

questions: why use subnets instead of more network numbers
subtitle: How one Internet network number can be split into several subnets, one per cable, without bloating routing tables.

tldr.problem: Organizations with several LAN cables had to either buy a network number for every cable, which bloated Internet routing tables, or hide the cables behind bridges, which does not work for every LAN technology.
tldr.mechanism: Split the local part of the Internet address into a subnet number and a host number, with a subnet field width that is constant for a given network. Hosts keep a 32-bit mask to tell local subnet traffic from traffic that needs a gateway, and an ICMP request and reply pair lets them learn the field width.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a proposal that asked for discussion and suggestions. It describes subnetting as a modest change to IP implementations that stays compatible with hosts on non-subnetted networks.

facts.label: Host mask example
facts.value: 255.255.0.0 for Class A with an 8-bit subnet field

today: RFC 917 is a proposal from October 1984 that asked for discussion and suggestions; the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text builds on RFC 791 (IP) and RFC 792 (ICMP) and refers to RFC 919 for broadcasting.

sections.title: Why One Network Needs Several Subnets
sections.content:
The original view of the Internet had two levels: the whole catenet, and below it a set of Internet networks, each with its own network number. That view treats a network as a single edge, a black box with hosts attached. It holds for the ARPANET and for most LANs such as Ethernet, but moderately large organizations often need more than one cable. The memo notes that Stanford University had eighteen cables in use at the time of writing.

The RFC lists four reasons for several cables: different LAN technologies, limits on hosts and cable length, congestion that is relieved by putting chatty groups of hosts on separate cables, and point-to-point links between distant parts of a campus.

An organization then has three choices. It can acquire a network number for each cable, which causes an explosion in the size of Internet routing tables and spreads purely local detail everywhere. It can use one number with host numbers assigned without regard to the LAN (transparent subnets), which relies on bridges and does not work for every LAN technology. Or it can use one number and give each LAN a subnet number (explicit subnets). The memo favors the third, because it modifies IP but remains compatible with existing hosts on non-subnetted networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If every street in town needed its own zip code, the post office's list would get huge. It is simpler to keep one zip code and number the streets inside it.

sections.title: Interpreting the Internet Address
sections.content:
The RFC weighs four ways to mark the subnet part of the local address: a variable-width field, a fixed-width field, and self-encoding versions of each. It rejects self-encoding schemes, because they cut the local address space by at least a factor of two and tie the subnet decision to how host numbers were already assigned. It chooses a variable-width subnet field.

The address is read as <network-number><subnet-number><host-number>. The host number must be at least one bit wide, and the subnet field width is constant for a given network. A width of zero means the network is not subnetted. The subnet field is the most significant part of the local address, and the memo sees little reason to subnet Class C networks because their local part is so small. It expects most sites to pick a multiple of eight bits, but implementations must handle other widths.

The memo also rejects recursive subnets (splitting the host field again), because there is no obvious need for four levels, there are too few address bits, and the extra mechanism is complex.
sections.plainLanguage: An address becomes three parts: which neighborhood, which street, which house. How many digits the street part gets is decided once for the whole neighborhood.

sections.title: Host Changes and Broadcasts
sections.content:
Normally an IP host compares the network number of the destination with its own to decide whether to send directly or via a gateway. To support subnets it stores one more 32-bit value, my_ip_mask, with bits set for the network number and the subnet field. For a Class A network with an eight-bit subnet field, the mask is 255.255.0.0. The host then compares the destination and its own address after a bitwise AND with the mask. A multi-homed host keeps an address and mask per interface.

Subnets add a broadcast case. Implementations must recognize three kinds of broadcast address besides their own: 255.255.255.255 for this physical network, which no gateway may forward; a specific network, with the local part all ones (for example 36.255.255.255); and a specific subnet, with the host field all ones (for example 36.40.255.255). A single operation can reach every host of a subnetted network, which the memo counts as an argument for subnets. The RFC points to RFC 919 for broadcasting.
sections.plainLanguage: A host keeps a stencil. Laid over its own address and a friend's address, the stencil shows whether they live on the same street or the message must go through the gateway.

sections.title: Learning the Subnet Field Width
sections.content:
A host can learn the field width from hardwired information, such as a disk file, or by asking over the network. Diskless workstations cannot rely on a file, so the memo proposes two new ICMP message types: Address Format Request (type A1) and Address Format Reply (type A2). A booting host broadcasts a request, and a gateway, or a host acting in lieu of one, answers with the width in the Code field. The width can be from 0 to 31 minus N, where N is the network number width (8, 16 or 24). If the request has source address zero, the reply is broadcast, though the RFC says this should be kept to a minimum.

If no answer arrives, the safest assumption is a width of zero. A host that guessed wrong should adjust when a gateway later broadcasts a reply that disagrees. Nobody should send a reply based on a guessed value. Using the protocol is optional, and a host with stable storage may use stored information instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A new kid asks, 'How many digits are in a street number here?' Any grown-up on the block can answer, and everyone gives the same answer.

sections.title: Subnet Routing and Existing Hosts
sections.content:
Subnets make routing two-level: within the network only subnet gateways matter, and toward another network a host must pick a gateway out and a path to it. Many hosts avoid this by using a default gateway and ICMP Host Redirect messages. The one step that must know about subnets is deciding whether the destination is on the same physical network.

Some unmodified implementations can still be used on subnetted networks, under conditions: single-homed hosts only, a broadcast LAN, ARP, and no need to keep connections alive if a gateway crashes. The trick is ARP-based subnetting. A subnet gateway answers an ARP request with its own hardware address when it is on the best route to the target, then forwards the packets. The memo admits this blurs layers, and that a connection breaks if the gateway crashes. It also stresses this differs from ARP-based bridges, and an ARP server should never answer a request whose target is a broadcast address, to avoid forwarding loops.

Case studies describe Stanford (subnets in use since early 1982, about 330 hosts and 18 subnets), MIT (one network number, with the 24-bit rest field split into three 8-bit fields) and Carnegie-Mellon (a Class B network with 11 physical subnets, using ARP-based bridges).
sections.plainLanguage: If a friend does not know about streets, the gateway can wave and say 'give it to me, I'll take it there.' It works, but it only works while that one gateway stays awake.
